title: The kingdom splits (1 Kings 12)
hookLine: a young king ignores the old counselors and the kingdom tears in two

lines: THY FATHER MADE OUR YOKE GRIEVOUS.
cards: "Thy father made our yoke grievous." Solomon is dead, and his son Rehoboam has gone to Shechem to be made king.

The people bring one request, in the King James words: make the heavy yoke your father put on us lighter, "and we will serve thee." That's the deal on the table. Lighten the load, and you have a kingdom.
Rehoboam doesn't answer on the spot. He tells them to come back in three days. And in those three days he asks for advice twice, from two very different tables.

teach.h: BE A SERVANT UNTO THIS PEOPLE.
teach.b: First he goes to the old men who stood before his father Solomon while he lived.
Their answer is a paradox: "If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever."
Serve them today, and they'll serve you for good. Then he goes to the young men who grew up with him. Their answer is the opposite: talk tough.
"My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins."
And: "my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions."

teach.h: HE FORSOOK THE COUNSEL OF THE OLD MEN.
teach.b: The text puts the choice in one line: he "forsook the counsel of the old men." He asked the old ones first, heard the answer, set it aside, and asked again.
On the third day he gives the people the young men's speech, word for word.
And the people answer with a cry that tears the kingdom: "What portion have we in David? ... to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David."
The northern tribes walk away and make Jeroboam their king; only Judah stays with the house of David. The text holds two things together. Rehoboam made a choice.
And "the cause was from the LORD," fulfilling a word a prophet had already spoken. Readers weigh those two lines differently, but nobody in the story pretends the choice wasn't his.
The old men's advice cost nothing but pride: one soft answer, one lighter yoke. He couldn't pay it.

how: Some Christians read Rehoboam's story as a warning about pride and about choosing advisers who only say what we want, and the old men's counsel to be a servant is sometimes linked to Jesus's teaching on servant leadership.

12:20: none followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only.

games.q: you're Rehoboam, about to be made king. the old men say: serve the people and speak good words, and they'll serve you forever. your friends say: be harder than your father. what do you do?
o: ask the people to wait another year.
games.why: he forsook the counsel of the old men and promised scorpions instead of whips. the people answered: to your tents, O Israel.

practice: Hold one decision that's in front of you, and then bring to mind someone older who has seen more of life than you: a parent, a grandparent, a neighbor, a retired coworker.
Hear, as honestly as you can, what they'd probably say, and ask yourself: is that the answer I'm avoiding? If you pray, bring both the decision and the person before God.

wordCard.voice: Rehoboam. The young king who heard the old men say be a servant, chose the young men's threat instead, and watched the people go to their tents.

orig.note: Hebrew: old men, elders, the counselors who had stood before Solomon (1 Kings 12:6).
